title: Celsus and the thirty-six Egyptian demons
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Κέλσος τοιαῦτα· ὅτι μὴν ἐν τοῖσδε μέχρι τῶν ἐλαχίστων ἔστιν ὅτῳ δέδοται ἐξουσία. μάθοι τις ἂν ἐξ ὧν Αἰγύπτιοι λέγουσιν. ὅτι ἄρα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ σῶμα ἓξ καὶ τριάκοντα διειληφότες δαίμονες ἢ θεοί τινες αἰθέριοι εἰς τοσαῦτα μέρη νενεμημένον (οἱ δὲ καὶ πολὺ πλείους λέγουσιν) ἄλλος ἄλλο τι αὐτοῦ νέμειν ἐπιτέτακται. καὶ τῶν δαιμόνων ἴσασι τὰ ὀνόματα ἐπιχωρίῳ φωνῇ, ὥσπερ Χνουμὴν καὶ Χναχουμὴν καὶ Κνὰτ καὶ Σικὰτ καὶ Βιοὺ καὶ Ἐροὺ καὶ Ἐρεβίου καὶ Ῥαμανὸρ καὶ Ῥειανοὸρ ὅσα τε ἄλλα τῇ ἑαυτῶν γλώσσῃ ὀνομάζουσι· καὶ δὴ ἐπικα λοῦντες αὐτοὺς ἰῶνται τῶν μερῶν τὰ παθήματα. τί ουν κωλύει τούτους τε καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους δεξιούμενον, ἂν χρῄζῃ τις, ὑγιαίνειν μᾶλλον ἢ νοσεῖν καὶ εὐτυχεῖν μᾶλλον ἢ δυστυχεῖν καὶ βασανιστηρίων καὶ κολαστηρίων ὡς οἷόν τε ἀπηλλάχθαι; καὶ διὰ τούτων δὴ κατάγειν ἡμῶν πειρώμενος τὴν ψυχὴν ὁ Κέλσος ἐπὶ τοὺς δαίμονας, ὡς λαχόντας ἡμῶν τὰ σώματα, καὶ ἕνα ἕκαστον ἐπιστατεῖν ἀποφαινόμενος μέρους τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν θέλει ἡμᾶς πιστεύειν μὲν οἷς λέγει δαιμονίοις καὶ θεραπεύειν αὐτὰ, ἵνα ὑγιαίνωμεν μᾶλλον ἢ νοσῶμεν καὶ εὐτυχῶμεν μᾶλλον ἢ δυστυχῶμεν καὶ ὅση δύναμις βασανιστηρίων, ὡς οἷόν τε ἐστὶν, ἀπαλλαγῶμεν, τοσοῦτον δ᾿ ἄρα κατέγνωκε τῆς εἰς τὸν θεὸν τῶν ολων ἀσχίστου καὶ ἀδιαιρέτου τιμῆς, ὡς μὴ αὐτάρκη πιστεύων τὸν θεὸν μόνον προσκυνούμενον καὶ μεγαλοφώνως τιμώμενον παρέχειν τῷ τιμῶντι ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ σέβειν αὐτὸν δύναμιν κωλυτικὴν τῆς τῶν δαιμόνων κατὰ τοῦ ὁσίου ἐπιβουλῆς· οὐ γὰρ ἑώρακε. τίνα τρόπον τὸ ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὑπὸ τῶν γνησίως πιστευόντων καλούμενον οὐκ ὀλίγους ἀπὸ νόσων καὶ δαιμονισμῶν καὶ ἄλλων περιστάσεων ἰάσατο.
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus says (φημί) such things: that indeed in these things down to the least (ἐλάχιστος) there is to whom authority (ἐξουσία) has been given (δίδωμι), one may learn (μανθάνω) from what the Egyptians (Αἰγύπτιοι) say: that thirty-six demons (δαίμονες) or certain ethereal gods (θεοὶ αἰθέριοι), having divided (διαλαμβάνω) the body (σῶμα) of man, apportioned (νέμω) into so many parts (μέρη) (others say even many more), one has been appointed (ἐπιτάσσω) to tend (νέμω) one part of it, another another. And they know the names (ὀνόματα) of the demons in the native tongue (ἐπιχώριος φωνή): Chnoumen, Chnachoumen, Knat, Sikat, Biou, Erou, Erebiou, Ramanor, Reianoor, and as many others as they name in their own language (γλῶσσα); and calling upon (ἐπικαλέω) them they heal (ἰάομαι) the sufferings (παθήματα) of the parts. What then prevents (κωλύω) one greeting / paying respects to (δεξιόομαι) these and the others, if one needs, to be healthy (ὑγιαίνω) rather than sick (νοσέω), fortunate (εὐτυχέω) rather than unfortunate (δυστυχέω), and to be freed (ἀπαλλάσσω) as far as possible from tortures (βασανιστήρια) and punishments (κολαστήρια)? And through these things Celsus, trying to bring down (κατάγω) our soul (ψυχή) to the demons, as having obtained by lot (λαγχάνω) our bodies, and declaring (ἀποφαίνομαι) that each one presides (ἐπιστατέω) over a part of our body, wants us to believe (πιστεύω) the demons (δαιμόνια) he speaks of and serve (θεραπεύω) them, that we may be healthy rather than sick and fortunate rather than unfortunate and, as much power as there is, be freed from tortures as far as possible; so much then he has condemned (καταγιγνώσκω) the unsplit (ἄσχιστος) and undivided (ἀδιαίρετος) honour (τιμή) toward the God of the universe (θεὸς τῶν ὅλων), as not believing that God alone, worshipped (προσκυνέω) and honoured with great voice (μεγαλοφώνως), suffices (αὐτάρκης) to give the one honouring, from the very revering (σέβω) Him, a power preventing (δύναμις κωλυτική) the plotting (ἐπιβουλή) of the demons against the holy one (ὅσιος); for he has not seen in what way that which is called in the name of Jesus (ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ) by those who genuinely (γνησίως) believe has healed not a few from diseases (νόσοι), demon-possessions (δαιμονισμοί) and other troubles (περιστάσεις).
pass_b_english: After this Celsus says words to this effect: “That in these matters, down to the very least, there is someone to whom authority has been given, one may learn from what the Egyptians say. They say that thirty-six demons, or certain ethereal gods, have divided the human body among them, apportioned into that many parts (some say far more), and each has been charged to tend a different part of it. They also know the names of the demons in their native tongue, such as Chnoumen, Chnachoumen, Knat, Sikat, Biou, Erou, Erebiou, Ramanor and Reianoor, and all the others they name in their own language; and by calling on them they heal the ailments of the parts. What then prevents anyone who so wishes from paying his respects to these and to the others, and so being healthy rather than sick, fortunate rather than unfortunate, and set free, as far as possible, from tortures and punishments?”

With these words Celsus tries to drag our soul down to the demons, as though they had received our bodies as their allotted portion, and he declares that each one presides over a part of our body. He wants us to trust the demons he speaks of and to serve them, so that we may be healthy rather than sick, fortunate rather than unfortunate, and be released from tortures to the full extent that it can be done. Yet so low is his opinion of the whole and undivided honour paid to the God of all that he does not believe that God alone, worshipped and honoured with a loud voice, is enough to give the one who honours Him, from the very act of revering Him, a power that holds back the plots of the demons against the devout. For he has not seen how the invocation of the name of Jesus by those who truly believe has healed not a few people from diseases, from possession by demons, and from other afflictions.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words run from ‘That in these matters’ to ‘tortures and punishments’; Koetschau’s stop after ἐξουσία is read as a pause inside one sentence (the ὅτι clause is the object of μάθοι). The demon names are transliterated from the Greek as printed (Χνουμήν, Χναχουμήν, Κνάτ, Σικάτ, Βιού, Ἐρού, Ἐρεβίου, Ῥαμανόρ, Ῥειανοόρ); these are the Egyptian decan names, and the spellings are kept without emendation. δεξιούμενον rendered ‘paying his respects to’ (lit. ‘greeting with the right hand’). ὅση δύναμις ... ὡς οἷόν τε ἐστίν is a doubled limiting phrase, merged as ‘to the full extent that it can be done’. τὸ ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ... καλούμενον rendered ‘the invocation of the name of Jesus’. No explicit Scripture quotation; healing in the name of Jesus may echo Mark 16:17 or Acts 3:6, but no single verse is clear, so none is cited. Review: ἀσχίστου καὶ ἀδιαιρέτου qualify τιμῆς (the honour, ‘whole and undivided’), not God; ‘undistracted’ was not the sense of ἄσχιστος. διειληφότες has the demons as subject, so the clause is active.
Celsus's Egyptian clause made active: the demons divided the body among them (διειληφότες)
ἀσχίστου καὶ ἀδιαιρέτου moved to the honour ('whole and undivided honour'); dropped wrong 'undistracted'
μὲν ... δ᾿ ἄρα contrast restored with 'Yet'
μεγαλοφώνως 'with full voice' to 'with a loud voice'; τοῦ ὁσίου 'the holy man' to 'the devout'
δεξιούμενον ... ὑγιαίνειν: 'and so being healthy' keeps the infinitive as the main verb; τοιαῦτα 'words to this effect'
